```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE, comment = "#>")
```

Three finished research guides, each built from a familiar dataset with a few
lines of code. Open one to see what `create_rg()` produces, then read the code
below it to see how little it took.

| Guide | Data | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| [Baseball players](../examples/baseball.html) | `dg_baseball`, shipped with datagoodr | messy as-entered text: written dates, `$851,950` salaries, coded levels |
| [Star Wars characters](../examples/starwars.html) | `dplyr::starwars` | list columns (films, vehicles) and missing values |
| [Motor Trend cars](../examples/mtcars.html) | `datasets::mtcars` | a small numeric dataset with 0/1 codes retyped as true/false |

The links open the guides on the package website; they are built by
`data-raw/example-guides.R` in the source repository.

## How a research guide is laid out

Every guide opens with a numbered contents list, then groups the variables by
data type (Boolean, Categorical, Numeric, Text, Identifier, Temporal). Each
variable is one unit:

- **Left rail** -- its data mode and data type (in orange), its plain-language
  label, its name, its description, and a PROPERTIES table (rows, distinct
  values, missing, zeros).
- **Right column** -- a graphic for its type (histogram, treemap, word cloud,
  true/false bars, calendar), a PREVIEW of its values, and its stats: quantiles
  and distribution shape for numbers, factor levels for categories, the most
  common values for text.

This is the default `"rail"` style. `create_rg(style = "compact")` draws the
same units condensed for documentation -- the properties table becomes a
one-row strip above the graphic, the preview and the long tables are kept
short, and the whitespace is roughly halved. The original three-column grid is
still available as `create_rg(style = "vintage")`.

## Baseball players

`dg_baseball` holds the 678 players who debuted in 2010-2014, with every column
exactly as it arrived. `dg_baseball_dictionary` supplies a label and description
for each column; `create_dgf()` takes them through `dd_vlabel` and `dd_vdesc`.

```{r}
library(datagoodr)

dd  <- dg_baseball_dictionary
dgf <- create_dgf(dg_baseball,
                  dd_vlabel = dd$label,
                  dd_vdesc  = dd$description,
                  dir = "baseball")
```

The `bats` and `throws` codes read better with their meanings. Level labels live
in the DGF's `dd_f_levels` column (a level/label table), which you can edit in
Excel or set in code before rendering:

```{r}
i <- match("bats", dgf$var_name)
dgf$dd_f_levels[i] <- jsonlite::toJSON(data.frame(
  level = c("R", "L", "B"),
  label = c("R (right)", "L (left)", "B (both)")))

create_rg(dgf, dir = "baseball", render = TRUE)
```

[Open the baseball guide](../examples/baseball.html)

## Star Wars characters

No preparation at all: `create_dgf()` collapses list columns such as `films` to
`a|b|c` text and profiles the rest.

```{r}
dgf <- create_dgf(dplyr::starwars, dir = "starwars")
create_rg(dgf, dir = "starwars", render = TRUE)
```

[Open the Star Wars guide](../examples/starwars.html)

## Motor Trend cars

`mtcars` keeps the car names in its row names, so split them into `make` and
`model` first. Its `vs` and `am` columns are 0/1 codes that the type guess reads
as counts; `retype_dgf()` turns them into true/false variables, and level labels
give the codes their meaning.

```{r}
cars <- data.frame(make  = sub(" .*", "", rownames(mtcars)),
                   model = sub("^\\S+ ?", "", rownames(mtcars)),
                   lapply(mtcars, as.character))

dgf <- create_dgf(cars, dir = "mtcars")
dgf <- retype_dgf(dgf, cars, types = c(vs = "boolean", am = "boolean"))

i <- match("am", dgf$var_name)
dgf$dd_f_levels[i] <- jsonlite::toJSON(data.frame(
  level = c("0", "1"), label = c("0 (automatic)", "1 (manual)")))

create_rg(dgf, dir = "mtcars", render = TRUE)
```

The full script, with labels and descriptions for every column, is
`data-raw/example-guides.R`.

[Open the Motor Trend guide](../examples/mtcars.html)
